calc_k_note: K accounts for end effect and wire insulation: 0.95 for bare wire (formula 142.5/f), about 0.92–0.93 for insulated wire.
calc_dipole_tip1: Cut each leg ~3–5 % longer and trim until the SWR minimum falls on the chosen frequency.
calc_dipole_tip2: Inverted V (90–120° angle): start with the same dimensions – it usually needs shortening by a few percent.
calc_dipole_tip3: Impedance about 50–75 Ω; a 1:1 current balun at the feed point limits currents on the braid.
calc_efhw_tip1: Start with a wire ~3 % longer and trim on the lowest band; set the higher bands with the capacitor at the transformer.
calc_efhw_tip2: The coax braid often acts as the counterpoise – a choke about 0.05 λ from the transformer keeps RF out of the shack.
calc_gp_tip1: Radials sloping at about 45° give about 50 Ω; horizontal ones about 36 Ω (SWR ~1.4).
calc_gp_tip2: Radials lying on the ground need not be resonant – the more, the better.
calc_gp_tip3: Tune with the radiator length; leave the radials slightly longer.
calc_jpole_feed: C – feed point from the bottom
calc_jpole_tip1: Move the feed point (C) up/down looking for the SWR minimum – this is the main adjustment.
calc_jpole_tip2: Resonance is set by the length of element A; B has less influence.
calc_jpole_tip3: A choke (a few turns) on the cable below the antenna helps – a J-pole likes currents on the braid.
calc_yagi_tip1: Starting dimensions for tube elements; gain typically 7–8 dBi, front-to-back ratio 15–20 dB.
calc_yagi_tip2: The driven element has an impedance of about 20–30 Ω – matching is needed (gamma, hairpin, beta).
calc_yagi_tip3: For a specific tube diameter it is best to recalculate the design in software (e.g. YagiCAD, 4nec2).
calc_moxon_tip1: L.B. Cebik's formulas (dependent on wire diameter) – fed directly with 50 Ω coax at the top (driven element).
calc_moxon_tip2: Gain about 5.5–6 dBi, very good front-to-back ratio; keep gap C exact.
calc_moxon_tip3: Insulated wire behaves like a thicker, “slower” one – shorten the dimensions by 2–3 %.
calc_loop_tip1: Formula 306.3/f (1005/f ft) for wire; impedance about 100–120 Ω.
calc_loop_tip2: Matching to 50 Ω: a λ/4 section of 75 Ω coax (“Cable sections” tab).
calc_loop_tip3: Fed at the bottom – horizontal polarisation; at a corner/side – vertical.
calc_stub_tip1: A λ/4 section shorted at the end acts like an open circuit – a filter/trap for that frequency.
calc_stub_tip2: Length measured connector to connector, including the connectors; check with an analyser.
calc_q_tip: E.g. 50 Ω ↔ 112 Ω: 75 Ω cable; a quad loop (~110 Ω) is matched with a 75 Ω section.
calc_swr_tip1: SWR up to 1.5 makes no difference to range; at SWR 2 you lose about 0.5 dB (11 % of the power).
calc_swr_tip2: A measurement at the radio shows SWR “improved” by cable loss – a long, lossy cable masks a bad match.
calc_gain_note: Dipole = 2.15 dBi (0 dBd); GP ≈ 1–2 dBi; 3-el Yagi ≈ 7–8 dBi. Calculate cable loss in “Cable loss”.
calc_power_tip1: Every 3 dB doubles the power; 1 S-meter unit (S) ≈ 6 dB, i.e. 4× the power.
calc_power_tip2: The licence sets the transmitter output power – ERP is useful e.g. for assessing EM field exposure.
calc_battery_tip1: TX current depends on power: a 100 W radio draws about 18–22 A, 10 W about 2–3 A, QRP 5 W about 1–1.5 A.
calc_battery_tip2: In winter battery capacity drops by as much as 20–30 %; do not discharge AGM below 50 %.

It is received most reliably by cable from the radio's audio output; through the microphone the 4-QAM and 16-QAM modes work in quiet surroundings. Tap a picture to save or share it.

location_rationale_text: Your position is used to work out your QTH locator, find the nearest repeaters and APRS stations, and calculate satellite passes and distances to DX stations. gl_legend: The yellow line is the gray line. The red dot is your QTH.
gl_about_text:
The gray line (terminator) is the band along the boundary between day and night. The ionosphere behaves in a special way there – the D layer (which absorbs lower frequencies) fades before nightfall, while the F layers stay ionised enough to reflect radio waves.

Thanks to this, stations lying on the same gray line can make unusually long DX contacts (gray-line propagation) on 160 m, 80 m or 40 m with minimal signal loss.

rst_r_scale:
1 – Unreadable
2 – Barely readable, occasional words
3 – Readable with considerable difficulty
4 – Readable with practically no difficulty
5 – Perfectly readable
rst_s_scale:
1 – Faint, signals barely perceptible
2 – Very weak
3 – Weak
4 – Fair
5 – Fairly good
6 – Good
7 – Moderately strong
8 – Strong
9 – Very strong
rst_s_note: Reports such as S9+10 dB or S9+20 dB are common – they mean a signal above the scale (measured on the S-meter).
rst_t_scale:
1 – Sixty-cycle AC or less, very rough and broad
2 – Very rough AC, very harsh and broad
3 – Rough AC tone, rectified but not filtered
4 – Rough note, some trace of filtering
5 – Filtered rectified AC but strongly ripple-modulated
6 – Filtered tone, definite trace of ripple modulation
7 – Near pure tone, trace of ripple modulation
8 – Near perfect tone, slight trace of modulation
9 – Perfect tone, no trace of ripple or modulation of any kind
